title: 13-layer HfO2-SiO2-Cr interference absorber on Al substrate
scientific_hypothesis: A 13-layer stack with Cr absorber layers positioned at electric field antinodes in the visible band will achieve higher absorptance in 400-700 nm while dielectric quarter-wave pairs maintain reflectance in 700-2000 nm.
design_principle: Recalled thin-film interference theory: metallic layers absorb where the standing wave electric field is strongest; dielectric pairs with quarter-wave optical thickness create high-reflectance bands at design wavelengths. Placing Cr at interference maxima in the visible while keeping dielectric thicknesses tuned for IR reflectance should produce the desired spectral split.
proposed_topology: air / hfo2 / sio2 / cr / hfo2 / sio2 / cr / hfo2 / sio2 / cr / hfo2 / sio2 / cr / hfo2 / al
soft_objectives: maximize mean absorptance in 400-700 nm band
maximize mean reflectance in 700-2000 nm band
maintain total layer count at exactly 13
manufacturing_considerations: Cr layers should remain thin (10-50 nm range) to avoid excessive visible absorption that would kill IR reflectance
Dielectric layers typically 50-300 nm for quarter-wave behavior across visible-IR
Total stack thickness should remain practical for coating processes
theory_basis: Recalled: Quarter-wave dielectric stacks produce high reflectance bands centered at design wavelength
Recalled: Metallic layers absorb proportionally to local electric field intensity squared
Recalled: HfO2 has higher refractive index than SiO2, creating useful index contrast for interference
Recalled: Cr has moderate extinction coefficient in visible, useful for controlled absorption without complete opacity
Recalled: Al substrate provides baseline IR reflectance that the stack should preserve
expected_advantages: Multiple Cr layers distributed through stack allow absorption at multiple field maxima
Dielectric pairs between Cr layers can tune interference to enhance visible field at absorber positions
13 layers provides sufficient degrees of freedom for spectral shaping while staying under 20-layer limit
known_risks: Cr material name may not resolve in registry - if rejected, would need to use exact measurement name from rejection list
Recalled quarter-wave thickness formula (lambda/4n) is approximate; actual optimal thickness depends on full stack interaction
Uncertain whether 13 layers is optimal vs 11 or 15 - this is a design choice not verified against literature
Cr extinction coefficient dispersion across 400-2000 nm is recalled but not checked against actual dataset
The specific sequence of Cr placement (every 3rd layer) is a hypothesis that may not be optimal
Would need to look up actual n/k dispersion data for hfo2, sio2, and cr to confirm absorption behavior
execution_request_english: Optimize a 13-layer planar multilayer film on aluminum substrate. Stack sequence from air side: hfo2, SiO2 (Lemarchand), Cr (Rakic-LD), hfo2, SiO2 (Lemarchand), Cr (Rakic-LD), hfo2, SiO2 (Lemarchand), Cr (Rakic-LD), hfo2, SiO2 (Lemarchand), Cr (Rakic-LD), hfo2, then Al (Rakic-LD) substrate. All 13 film layer thicknesses are design variables with bounds 10-400 nm. Illumination: normal incidence, unpolarized, wavelength range 400-2000 nm. Objectives: maximize absorptance in 400-700 nm band, maximize reflectance in 700-2000 nm band. Use coherent transfer matrix method solver. Material names: hfo2, SiO2 (Lemarchand), Cr (Rakic-LD), Al (Rakic-LD).
revision_reason: Continuation of control arm with refined focus on layers 4 and 10 based on observed resonance behavior in prior rounds
